summary:
Zonguldak is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework set out below. The source inventory records no trans-specific statute, enforcement series, arrest pattern or incident for Zonguldak itself. That absence indicates no documented divergence from national practice rather than local safety: a visitor to Zonguldak remains subject to Turkey's national rules, its document checks and its policing patterns.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", carrying up to three years in prison, and would criminalise participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies, carrying up to four years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft. Human Rights Watch warned that the measures would force LGBT life underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, surgery included, from 18 to 25, conditioned on mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible.

Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people hardened into explicit state policy during the year. Year of the Family instructions were issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed for the first time in years, expression and artistic freedom were restricted, and events were cancelled or banned.

The same review records 6 violations of the right to life, including 3 hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected; 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year; and 313 violations of liberty, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total, comprising 299 detention decisions.

Private-life violations rose from 16 to 67, among them obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy, and the review documents 61 travel bans. Both sources report at national level with no provincial breakdown, so these counts cannot be attributed to Zonguldak; they describe the enforcement environment a trans visitor enters anywhere in Turkey.
tangentialFactors:
Neither source disaggregates by province, so Zonguldak cannot be ranked against any other Turkish province on detention, travel-ban or violence counts. What the national series establish is direction rather than a fixed level: torture and ill-treatment violations rose from 51 to 89 in a year, and private-life violations from 16 to 67, with the growth concentrated in categories that touch trans life directly, including hormone therapy.

The draft measures and the recorded enforcement sit in different legislative states. The 11th Judicial Package remained a leaked proposal when Human Rights Watch reported it, whereas the detentions, travel bans and institutional closures counted by Kaos GL took place under existing authority. A visitor therefore faces documented action now, with a further layer of penalties still pending rather than in force.

Institutional opposition is documented but has not altered the pattern. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association challenged the draft, and the review still records an organisation closed and events banned, indicating that professional and civil-society objections have not checked the policy direction.

The 61 travel bans recorded in a single year bear directly on movement across borders and internal transit, and they form part of a package of liberty violations that also produced 299 detention decisions.
localsOnly:
Residents of Zonguldak live under the same national penal framework as the rest of Turkey, and the pending 11th Judicial Package would add offences aimed at gender presentation and at participation in same-sex ceremonies, with prison terms of up to three and four years respectively. Until it is enacted, prosecutions proceed under the penal code as it stands.

Care access for trans residents is constrained by the draft's proposed age floor of 25 for gender-affirming care, backed by mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Clinicians face fines and up to seven years for performing such interventions, patients up to three years, which places both prescribing and receiving under threat.

The monitoring year recorded 299 detention decisions and 89 torture or ill-treatment violations nationwide, with private-life violations rising to 67 including obstruction of hormone therapy, and an LGBTI+ rights organisation closed. These are resident-facing measures: they fall on people living in Turkey, on its organisations and on its healthcare staff, and they are not contingent on the draft's passage.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted since the Human Rights Watch report of 29 October 2025 is unresolved in the inventory; the sources describe a draft, not a statute in force.

No policing record, arrest series, hate-crime incident, Pride or event ban, or healthcare directive specific to Zonguldak appears in the inventory. Whether any provincial health authority in Zonguldak has issued circulars of the kind reported elsewhere in Turkey is not sourced.

The Kaos GL counts — 6 right-to-life violations, 89 torture violations, 313 liberty violations, 299 detention decisions, 67 private-life violations, 61 travel bans — are national totals with no provincial distribution, so their allocation to Zonguldak is unresolved.

The inventory does not state how many detentions or travel bans involved foreign nationals, nor whether the draft's penalties would be applied to visitors as opposed to residents.
